summary.text: Take \(\epsilon=1/2\). For every threshold \(N\), choose a prime \(p\ge\max(N,81)\); the only admissible integers up to \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)=2\), while \(81>e^4\) implies \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\), contradicting the proposed eventual lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ divides }n\}.
\]
Equivalently, the set of prime factors of \(k\) must be a subset of the set of prime factors of \(n\). We disprove the assertion
\[
\forall \epsilon>0\;\exists N\;\forall n\ge N,
\qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n).
\]

The key observation is that \(a(n)\) is constant on prime arguments.

**Lemma.** If \(p\) is prime, then \(a(p)=2\).

Indeed, the prime factors of \(p\) form the singleton set \(\{p\}\). Consider an integer \(k\) such that \(1\le k\le p\) and every prime factor of \(k\) is a prime factor of \(p\).

There are two cases. If \(k=1\), then \(k\) is admissible because \(1\) has no prime factors, so its set of prime factors is vacuously a subset of \(\{p\}\). If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has at least one prime divisor, say \(q\). By the assumed containment of prime-factor sets, \(q\) must be a prime factor of \(p\), and hence \(q=p\). Thus \(p\mid k\). Since \(k\) is positive and \(k\le p\), the only possibility is \(k=p\). Conversely, \(p\) itself is plainly admissible. Therefore the admissible integers in \([1,p]\) are exactly \(1\) and \(p\), proving
\[
a(p)=2.
\]

We now choose the single value
\[
\epsilon=\frac12.
\]
For this value the proposed lower bound becomes
\[
(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}=(\log n)^{1/2}=\sqrt{\log n}.
\]
We will show that, beyond every proposed threshold \(N\), there is a prime \(p\ge N\) for which
\[
\sqrt{\log p}>2=a(p),
\]
which is the strict reverse of the conjectured inequality.

For a convenient explicit numerical threshold, note that
\[
e=\exp(1)<3.
\]
One elementary justification is the exponential series
\[
e=1+1+\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}\frac1{m!}.
\]
For \(m\ge2\), one has \(m!\ge 2^{m-1}\), and the inequality is strict once \(m\ge3\). Hence
\[
\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}\frac1{m!}
<\sum_{m=2}^{\infty}\frac1{2^{m-1}}=1,
\]
so \(e<3\). Consequently,
\[
\exp(4)=\exp(1)^4=e^4<3^4=81.
\]
It follows that whenever \(p\ge81\),
\[
\exp(4)<81\le p.
\]
Since the exponential function is strictly increasing and logarithm is its inverse on the positive reals, this gives
\[
4<\log p.
\]
Both sides are positive, so taking square roots preserves the strict inequality:
\[
2=\sqrt4<\sqrt{\log p}=(\log p)^{1/2}.
\]

It remains only to ensure that such a prime can be found beyond any prescribed \(N\). Primes are unbounded. For completeness, given any bound \(B\ge1\), consider \(B!+1>1\) and choose a prime divisor \(p\) of it. If \(p\le B\), then \(p\mid B!\), while also \(p\mid B!+1\), forcing \(p\mid1\), an impossibility. Thus \(p>B\). In particular, for any proposed threshold \(N\), apply this argument with
\[
B=\max\{N,81\}.
\]
There is then a prime \(p>B\), and hence certainly \(p\ge N\) and \(p\ge81\).

For this prime, the lemma gives \(a(p)=2\), while the logarithmic estimate gives
\[
(\log p)^{1-1/2}=\sqrt{\log p}>2=a(p).
\]
Thus the claimed inequality
\[
(\log p)^{1-1/2}\le a(p)
\]
fails.

We have therefore exhibited a fixed positive value \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) such that for every \(N\) there exists \(n\ge N\)—indeed, one may take an arbitrarily large prime \(n=p\)—for which
\[
(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}>a(n).
\]
This is exactly the negation of the proposed eventual lower bound, so the conjecture is false.
